extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents, and intellectual property office (IPO) examiners/staff in ASEAN Member States
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines on patent filing formalities, substantive examination prerequisites, and related procedures applicable across ASEAN Member States, covering required documents, language/translation, priority, fees, e-filing, amendments, unity, divisional practice, and grace periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language(s) of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must file their patent application, including the specification, in the official language of the country of filing (for Cambodia, Lao PDR, Indonesia, Thailand and Viet Nam) and English (for Brunei Darussalam and Singapore). In Malaysia, Myanmar and the Philippines, applicants can choose between the official language and English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The language of filing is the language of proceedings; translations of the specification (title, abstract, claims, description and drawings) must be filed within a specified period or upon request if filed in another language. In Myanmar, even if English is selected, office communications are in the country’s official language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for grant (application form) and minimum information
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for grant of a patent (application form) must be filed on the prescribed form (paper or electronically except where only electronic is accepted) and be accompanied by the prescribed official fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The request should indicate date of request, applicant details (name, address/place of business, sometimes nationality), inventor details, and may include resident agent/representative and applicant/agent signature where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title of the invention (formal requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the invention is a formal requirement and must be short and clearly indicate the subject matter to which the invention relates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract is a formal requirement that provides a summary of the invention and may be used for technical information and searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract must not be used to define the scope of protection sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description / enablement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must specify the technical field, indicate background art useful for understanding/search, disclose the invention clearly and in detail so a person skilled in the art can carry it out, disclose at least one mode of making/using the invention, and briefly describe figures/drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must contain one or more claims which define the matter for which protection is sought; claims must be clear and supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must define subject-matter in terms of technical features (which may be expressed in mathematical, structural and/or functional terms). Claims must not rely on references to the description or drawings for technical features unless necessary for understanding or to enhance clarity/conciseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where necessary, any drawing referred to in the description or in any claim must be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claim (12‑month rule and evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A national application may claim priority of an earlier application filed not more than 12 months before the filing date in a Paris Convention or WTO member state; the 12‑month period cannot be extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming priority, submit the priority document/certified copy (except Singapore where provided if requested) and sufficient evidence of entitlement within national timeframes. Multiple priorities may be claimed and the effective date for subject-matter is the earliest priority application that discloses it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claim invalidity and effect on prior art date
rubrics_metrics.description: A priority claim is invalid if made outside the 12‑month period or if the earlier application was not actually the first application by the applicant for the disclosed subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the priority claim is invalid, the effective filing date for determining prior art is the local filing date; other causes of invalidity are addressed during substantive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of attorney requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A power of attorney must be submitted if the patent applicant is not a resident of the country of filing and is represented by an agent (exceptions: Brunei Darussalam and Singapore where it's encompassed in the application form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If signed abroad, it may need notarization or certification depending on national provisions; power of attorney may be filed after filing or after receiving notice within periods prescribed by national law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment / statement of inventorship / declaration of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A deed of assignment/statement of inventorship/declaration of invention must be filed if ownership was transferred from inventor(s) to applicant(s) before the filing date, within periods prescribed by national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some AMS provide standard compulsory forms (Brunei, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore); notarization may be required in some countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation, certification, notarization or legalization of filing documents
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification is filed in a language other than the official/authorized language, a translation must be filed within a specified period or upon request. For priority documents, a certified copy must be filed (exception: Singapore). Notarization/certification of POA and assignment may be required in certain AMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check national provisions for exact periods and formalities (e.g., Cambodia, Lao PDR, Thailand, the Philippines have specific notarization requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Late filing options and maximum deadlines for documents
rubrics_metrics.description: AMS provide options for late filing of documents (claims, priority documents, power of attorney, assignment/declarations) within periods prescribed by national law or upon request of the office/Registrar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Singapore allows claims to be submitted within 12 months of priority date; submission timing and acceptability vary per AMS and per document type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation timing for PCT national phase applications
rubrics_metrics.description: For PCT national phase applications in many AMS, translation of the specification into an official/authorized language can be submitted after filing within the period prescribed by national provisions or upon request of the office/Registrar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicable to Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Viet Nam (check national provisions for deadlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple priority claims and fee implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple priorities from different countries may be claimed in one national application; where AMS charge a fee per priority claim, the fee must be paid for each priority claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The earliest application which discloses a subject-matter governs the priority date for that subject-matter; multiple priorities can provide different effective dates for different embodiments disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of filing fees (per application / per claim / per excess pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing fees in most AMS are calculated taking into account the number of claims and sometimes number of pages; Thailand is an exception charging per application irrespective of pages/claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds for excess claim fees vary (5 claims in Philippines to 25 in Brunei); Viet Nam applies excess fees to independent claims only. Excess claims/pages fees timing varies (payable at filing/search/grant depending on country). Some AMS also charge for excess pages (thresholds differ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic filing and online payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Most AMS use web-based filing; some offer both e-filing and paper filing, while some (e.g., Indonesia and Singapore) only accept electronic submission for certain filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-filing systems often allow online payment by credit card or online banking and are intended to streamline filing and publication; some documents (original certified copies) may still need original submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion between patent and utility model
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent or utility model (petty patent/simple patent/utility innovation) can be applied for based on a priority claim from the other; requests to convert from patent to utility model or vice versa can be filed in most AMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: Brunei Darussalam and Singapore do not have utility model protection. Conversion requests generally can be filed any time before grant or refusal in most AMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period provisions for pre-filing disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: All AMS operate a grace period (usually six to twelve months, most provide twelve months) during which certain disclosures by the inventor/applicant or predecessors are not considered prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace periods commonly cover inventor/applicant disclosures, some AMS exempt disclosures that are abuse of rights or breach of confidence; Philippines, Singapore and Viet Nam specifically cover disclosures made by the patent office; exhibitions may be covered with required certificates. Where an abstract published outside the grace period lacks enabling detail, novelty/inventive step may still be assessed during substantive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of non-prejudicial disclosure content
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration of non-prejudicial disclosure may include type of disclosure (applicant/inventor, third party lawful/unlawful disclosure, exhibition, paper/presentation), date, title and place of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices will assess filed evidence (statutory declarations/affidavits) to determine whether an earlier disclosure was by the inventors/applicants; some exceptions (e.g., Viet Nam) have different evidentiary handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalities examination required documents and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalities examination checks compliance with formal requirements: request form, applicant/inventor identification, title, description and one or more claims, drawings when necessary, abstract, representative details, priority claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contents of abstract, description, drawings, title and claims are not closely scrutinized during formalities beyond identifiability; however some AMS may examine initial clarity, multiple dependency, claim priority evaluation, exclusions to patentability or even unity 'a priori' during formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for rejection/abandonment during formalities examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications may be deemed abandoned or rejected if required filing documents are missing/erroneous/incomplete/non-compliant, if title/abstract/description/claims are missing, translations are not timely, foreign applicants are unrepresented when required, inventor designation/assignment missing, documents not filed in time, prescribed fees unpaid, or where non-patentable subject matter is present (country-specific).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners identify deficiencies and invite remedy within defined (possibly extendable) periods; failure to remedy leads to abandonment/rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of application before and during formalities examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may amend or correct the application/specification of their own initiative or at the request of the office, without affecting the filing date, provided they request to amend in the prescribed manner and within prescribed periods with any required documents/fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepted amendments are entered in the application and considered for publication. New matter extending beyond the originally filed disclosure will be rejected; applicants may broaden claims only within the scope of the originally filed disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment after completion of formalities (pre‑grant amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may request amendment of the specification after formalities completion, but pre-grant amendments must not result in inclusion of subject-matter extending beyond the originally filed application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic or paper filing of amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments can be filed electronically or on paper in most AMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: Singapore only allows amendments filed electronically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of unity of invention (a priori and a posteriori)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must relate to one invention or to a group of inventions linked to form a single general inventive concept; unity is assessed a priori (from claims language) and a posteriori (in view of the prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link must be a technical relationship expressed in claims via same/corresponding special technical features. Lack of unity should be determined from properly construed claim language and relevant prior art. Unity is best assessed during substantive examination but should be considered early to avoid unnecessary costs. Avoid narrow/literal approaches; use broad, practical consideration of interdependence. Example: independent claims A+Z, A+Y, Z+Y lack unity a priori if no common subject-matter; A+Z and A+Y have unity a priori while a posteriori lack may arise if A is known in prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional applications and lack of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: If unity of invention is lacking, the applicant must limit claims to overcome objection or may file divisional application(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether divisional can be proactively filed or only after an objection varies by AMS; except Myanmar and Thailand, divisionals can be filed voluntarily or at examiner request. Divisional subject-matter must not go beyond the initial disclosure. Claims of a divisional need not be limited to subject-matter already claimed in the parent (but watch double patenting issues).
